extracted.intended_audience: students and researchers in evolutionary biology, heredity, and statistical genetics
extracted.subtask_description: Assessing and distinguishing models of inheritance (blended vs exclusive), quantifying heredity intensities via correlations among relatives, and estimating the strength of natural selection versus non-selective mortality using pedigree/statistical data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Law of ancestral heredity (blended inheritance)
rubrics_metrics.description: A conception of inheritance in which each ancestor in the direct line contributes his quota, the whole heritage being a blend of such contributions from a long series proportioned in a perfectly definite manner; predicts regression toward the mean and gives coefficients for the contribution of successive ancestors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applies when characters are blended. Use the law to construct the probable character of an individual from a given ancestry (the first law applies to blended inheritance); numerical coefficients for contributions of parents, grandparents, etc., are provided. It predicts regression (offspring tending toward population mean) and gives expected correlation values for relatives under pangamy. Example/note: the law is used to compute how selection changes type over generations and how much ancestry contributes (e.g. series of factors like .6, .5, .25 etc in tables).

rubrics_metrics.name: Law of reversion (exclusive inheritance)
rubrics_metrics.description: A law applying to exclusive inheritance (offspring inherits the full character of either parent rather than a blend) that predicts the percentages of offspring reverting to each ancestral type; dominant feature is reversion rather than regression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply only when characters show exclusive inheritance. The law gives quotas (e.g. 25% follow parents, percentages for grandparents, great-grandparents, etc.) that describe distribution among the whole group of offspring rather than the expected character of an individual. Keep law of reversion distinct from law of ancestral heredity; it predicts distribution of reversion among offspring and is not the same as blended coefficients. The text cautions that observed data must first determine whether a character follows blended or exclusive inheritance before seeking reversion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish regression, reversion, and atavism (definitions & diagnostic criteria)
rubrics_metrics.description: Precise definitions: regression = phenomenon of blended inheritance (tendency toward population mean); reversion = full reappearance in an individual of a character recorded in a definite ancestor (has immediate ancestral history); atavism = return of an abnormal character not typical of the race but found in allied races (no immediate ancestral history).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To claim reversion or atavism, require precise ancestral evidence (a definite ancestor) and not confuse normal regression or extreme variation with reversion. Consider alternative explanations: (i) extreme normal variation, (ii) congenital malformation, (iii) skipping a generation (sex-linked transmission), (iv) normal regression misinterpreted, (v) changed environment effects, (vi) hybridization effects. Seek reversion primarily in exclusive inheritance; in blended characters reversion claims are generally unwarranted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expected coefficients for relatives under blended vs exclusive inheritance
rubrics_metrics.description: Theoretical numeric intensities (correlation coefficients) of inheritance for different relatives under blended (pangamy) and ideal exclusive inheritance (without/with reversion). Example table values: Parent-offspring blended ≈ .3; exclusive ≈ .5; grandparent blended ≈ .15; exclusive ≈ .25; further ancestors diminish by halves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these theoretical values to compare with observed correlations to infer the mode of inheritance. The text provides concrete numbers (and extended tables) for parent, grandparent, great-grandparent, uncle-nephew, and fraternal relationships, and shows how deviations may indicate reversion, prepotency, assortative mating, or sampling artifacts. Remember assumptions (equipotency of sexes, pangamy, no sexual selection).

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical test via correlation among relatives (use data to choose model)
rubrics_metrics.description: Test whether a character follows blended or exclusive inheritance by collecting large samples of relative pairs (parents-offspring, grandparents, avuncular, fraternal) and computing correlation coefficients; compare observed values to theoretical expectations for each model.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: eye-colour data (800–1,500 pairs per relation) produced parent-offspring correlation .4947, grandparent .3166, avuncular .2650, fraternal .4749; these fit exclusive inheritance better than blended, except fraternal relation which may be affected by family-size structure or prepotency. Use sufficient sample sizes, tabulation and reduction methods, and consider family-size (n) effects when interpreting fraternal correlations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of ancestry and selection when computing inherited proportions
rubrics_metrics.description: When computing how much of a selected character is transmitted to offspring, account for the ancestry of mid-parents (e.g. selecting mid-parents with non-mediator ancestry changes the expected transmitted fraction from .6H to .^Hl in the table example).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume naive multiplication of regression fractions across generations without accounting for selected ancestry of parents and grandparents. Explicit pedigree constants (e.g. table of pedigree stock constants) show how values vary with number of generations of record and ancestral assumptions. Clarify whether mid-parents beyond nth generation are assumed mediocre or unknown; this affects constants and predictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of selection intensity and number of generations on permanence of type
rubrics_metrics.description: Selection, when stringent, can establish a new permanent type within a few generations (examples: after four generations offspring may breed true to .9375 of the character; after six generations breed true within ~2% divergence).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use quantitative heredity estimates (e.g. heritability factors like .6 or .5) and generational models to calculate how many generations of selection are needed to fix a trait. Consider organism generation time: in humans, several generations correspond to centuries; in fast-breeding species, only a few years may suffice. Ensure selection is 'stringent'—natural selection typically selects around a type (preserving variability about it).

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits to reduction of population variability by selection
rubrics_metrics.description: Even indefinite selection cannot reduce the original variation of the race by more than a certain amount (stated as ~11% in the example); in nature reduction will be less because selection is around a type and preserves variability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When modeling long-term selection effects, account for theoretical maximum limits to variability reduction; avoid assuming selection can create arbitrarily large reductions in population variance. The third-column variabilities in the table become approximately correct only when selection is very stringent about the type.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method for estimating selective vs non-selective death-rates using sibling longevity correlations
rubrics_metrics.description: Estimate the proportion of deaths that are selective (function of constitution) versus non-selective by correlating ages at death of relatives (e.g., 1,000 pairs of brothers from the Peerage), excluding minors and using populations under similar environments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If there were no selective death-rate, ages at death of brothers would be uncorrelated; if no non-selective deaths, expect correlation ~.4 (value observed for stature etc.). Observed fraternal correlation .2602 (+-.0216) leads, by mixture-model reasoning, to estimate non-selective death-rate ≈ 20% and selective ≈ 80% of total death-rate. Steps: choose comparable-environment sample, exclude minors, compute correlation table as described earlier, compare to theoretical .4, and solve for mixture proportion. Beware of screening factors (correlated organs, age differences) and separate analyses (father-son gave different selective fraction ~65%).

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice of method to assess selection on longevity (organ-specific vs whole-complex approach)
rubrics_metrics.description: Two approaches: (1) test death-rate as function of the size of a particular organ; (2) take pairs of relatives with general resemblance (family members) and correlate their fitness/longevity as a proxy for the whole complex determining survival.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Method (1) is preferable if a single organ strongly determines vitality but is often confounded by correlated organs, growth and age differences. Method (2) avoids selecting a specific organ but may mix many factors; it assumes relatives share the relevant complex. Choose based on the trait and recognize limitations: correlated characters, age structure, and environmental homogeneity must be addressed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assumptions and caveats underlying theoretical expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: Calculations and tables assume equipotency of both sexes, pangamy (random mating), no sexual selection, and absence of assortative mating or within-marriage prepotency unless explicitly allowed for.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When observed correlations deviate from theory, consider relaxing or testing these assumptions: prepotency within individual marriages, homogamy (assortative mating), unequal sex potency, sampling biases, and reversion to distant ancestors. Use additional observations/experiments before accepting alternative laws (e.g., law of reversion requires further confirmation).
